citation.title: Multi-scale topology optimization of multi-material heterogeneous microstructures based on deep learning
citation.authors: Jiaxiang Luo, Yu Li, Weien Zhou, Zeyu Zhang, Wen Yao
citation.venue: Journal of Computational Design and Engineering 12(8) 127-153 (advance access 16 July 2025; CC BY-NC 4.0)
citation.arxiv_id: none found (arXiv title search returned no match)
citation.version_coded: Version of record: publisher PDF (27 pp.), read in full as text. curl received a bot challenge on academic.oup.com (not bypassed); WebFetch read the article page, whose PDF link redirected to the publisher's own PDF server (silverchair), from which the PDF was downloaded

included.reason: I-SPEED (screening code kept at full text; the only measured classical comparison is per property evaluation, a cost proxy as in P00149)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: The MLP surrogate returns a microstructure's homogenized elasticity tensor and volume fraction about 500× faster than numerical homogenization (≈6×10⁻⁴ s vs ≈0.32-0.34 s on five example microstructures), with MAE below 0.01.
claim.key_phrase: approximately 500 times faster than the homogenization theory
claim.location: Sec. 2.3, p. 134, and Table 2, p. 135 (first quantitative comparison with a classical method, in the main text; the abstract, introduction and conclusions state the cost saving only qualitatively)
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Stated in Sec. 2.3 as approximately 500×, per microstructure evaluation. Per-example ratios stated as 510, 557, 549, 570 and 486× for microstructures (6)-(10); they match Table 2 (e.g. 0.3190 s ÷ 6.251×10⁻⁴ s = 510 [derived]); mean of the five ratios 534 [derived]. Not an optimization-level speed-up: no classical multiscale TO is run or timed. Data generation and training are excluded.
claim.alternatives: (1) Abstract, qualitative: the surrogate substantially cuts the computational need for microstructure analysis. (2) Introduction, key features: offline mapping removes repeated calculations and substantially reduces computational time (qualitative). (3) Conclusions, qualitative: the single-training surrogate mitigates the burden of repeated real-time homogenization. No comparison of optimized designs or optimization run time with any classical TO exists; Table 3 per-iteration times (0.3 s at 16×8 to 3.79 s at 56×28) are for MMTO-DL only.

baseline.classical_method: Numerical homogenization (HC) of each 100×100-pixel microstructure, i.e. the online homogenization step that classical multiscale TO would repeat per cell and iteration (Sec. 2.3, Table 2; refs Guedes & Kikuchi 1990, Andreassen & Andreasen 2014, Dong et al. 2019). No classical optimizer is run
baseline.implementation: not stated for HC; the surrogate is built in Python/PyTorch (Sec. 2.3, 3.5)
baseline.hardware_classical: not stated for the Table 2 timing [inferred: the same i9-13900K workstation used for training, Sec. 2.3]
baseline.hardware_ml: 13th Gen Intel Core i9-13900K 3.00 GHz workstation, 64 GB memory, for surrogate training (Sec. 2.3) and all numerical examples (Sec. 4); no GPU mentioned
baseline.problem_size: Microstructure 100×100 pixels (Sec. 2.3) [≈2×10⁴ DOFs, derived]; macroscale meshes 16×8 to 56×28 (Table 3), mostly 32×16 (Sec. 4.1), 40×4 and 36×12 for shape matching (Sec. 4.2)
baseline.classical_iterations: not applicable: one homogenization per microstructure is timed; no classical optimization run
baseline.ml_time: Surrogate 6.251×10⁻⁴, 6.016×10⁻⁴, 6.013×10⁻⁴, 5.898×10⁻⁴ and 6.478×10⁻⁴ s (Table 2); MMTO-DL per-iteration time 0.3 s (16×8) to 3.79 s (56×28) (Sec. 4.1.3, Table 3)
baseline.training_time: 131 min for the selected model (batch 512, learning rate 1×10⁻², loss 2.2×10⁻³) (Sec. 2.3); the search over 25 hyperparameter combinations, 120 epochs each, is not timed
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated; 156,000 microstructures (6 heights sampled at 0.1 steps), each homogenized numerically at 100×100 pixels, split 132,600/23,400 (Sec. 2.3) [inferred ≈14 h at the Table 2 mean HC time of 0.327 s: 156,000 × 0.327 s ≈ 51,000 s]
baseline.quality_metric: MAE over the seven surrogate outputs (C11, C12, C13, C22, C23, C33, ve) against HC for five microstructures (Table 2); design level: compliance J and shape-matching displacement MSE computed with surrogate-predicted properties in the macroscale FE
baseline.quality_gap: MAE 0.0041, 0.0011, 0.0059, 0.0024 and 0.0066 for microstructures (6)-(10), all below 0.01 (Table 2). No design-level gap to a classical method exists

R1.evidence: Sec. 2.3 and Table 2: time and accuracy are reported for the same five microstructures, and the surrogate outputs sit within their reported error (MAE < 0.01) of HC. Matching is loose: the claim is per property evaluation; no classical multiscale TO is run, so neither design quality nor total optimization time is matched; the five examples are illustrative picks from Fig. 3B, and whether they lie in the training set is not stated. Coded as in P00149.

R2.evidence: Sec. 2.3, Table 2: HC implementation, solver and timing hardware are not stated; both methods ran on a CPU workstation [inferred], so (c) does not apply, and the problem has ≈2×10⁴ DOFs [derived], below 10⁵. The abstract gives no baseline figure (b); no iteration count applies (d); no per-iteration classical time exists (e). 0.32-0.34 s for one 100×100 homogenization shows no evident inefficiency. Unsure, so pass.

R3.evidence: Sec. 2.3: training time is reported (131 min, final model; hyperparameter search not timed), but the cost of homogenizing the 156,000 training microstructures is not [inferred ≈14 h at 0.327 s each]. No break-even is given; the introduction argues only qualitatively that the one-off data and training cost is repaid by reuse. C3 [derived]: (51,000 s + 7,860 s) ÷ (0.327 − 0.0006) s ≈ 1.8×10⁵ property evaluations, i.e. ≈350 iterations at 32×16 cells or ≈8 runs of the 40×4, 135-iteration shape-matching example.

R4.evidence: Table 2: surrogate outputs are checked against FE homogenization, but only for five illustrative microstructures; no held-out error is reported beyond the 2.2×10⁻³ loss value (Sec. 2.3). Design objectives (e.g. J = 16.676, Sec. 4.1.2; 19.455, 21.687, 17.580, Sec. 4.1.4) come from the macroscale FE with surrogate-predicted properties; the reconstructed structures are not re-analysed [inferred]. Volume is a soft penalty and final fractions are only plotted (Fig. 12A). One unreasonable design is noted qualitatively (Fig. 14(6)); no failure counts. A stricter reading (surrogate-predicted, selected examples) gives fail.

reporting.n_test_cases: 5 microstructures for the timing and accuracy comparison (Table 2). Optimization examples: mid-cantilever (1 run, Fig. 12; 9 volume-fraction cases, Fig. 13; 6 initial conditions, Fig. 14), Michell beam (6 material settings, Fig. 15; 6 mesh sizes, Table 3), 3 symmetry cases (Fig. 16), 3 non-design-domain cases (Fig. 17), shape matching (1 + 8 ratios, Figs. 18-19; 9 cases, Table 4)

notes: Stratum is a judgment call, coded as in P00149 (surrogate vs FE homogenization, per evaluation, accepted as a cost proxy). The article never runs, times or quotes a classical multiscale TO; the only measured classical comparison is surrogate vs numerical homogenization (Table 2). If the verifier rejects the per-evaluation proxy, no other classical comparison remains, and the next applicable code is FT-NOBASELINE (FT-FORWARD does not fit, because the networks also act as the optimizer via neural reparameterization). Qualitative mentions of other work (Sec. 3.5: non-linear fitting models called infeasible for 6+p parameters; Sec. 4.2: prior single-material shape matching) carry no numbers. Method: a per-problem reparameterization MLP (4 layers × 200 neurons, coordinates to 6 cutting heights and p material fractions, softmax with penalty factor) plus an offline MLP surrogate (6-24-128-24-7, ReLU, MAE loss, Adam) (Sec. 2.3-2.4, 4). Screening coded method_family neural_reparam; surrogate_mlp_gp is used here because the primary outcome concerns the surrogate. Baseline-strength note [inferred]: a classical parametrized multiscale TO could also precompute the database once and interpolate, which the article argues against qualitatively but does not time. The surrogate's analytic gradients replace sensitivities of the homogenized tensor; that saving is not quantified. Reporting: runtimes_all_cases = yes because all five Table 2 examples are timed; optimization runtimes appear only as per-iteration times in the mesh study (Table 3); timing protocol: hardware for training and examples stated (Sec. 2.3, 4), no repeats or warm-up. No code or data availability statement; a conflict-of-interest statement is present. OOD: none; the one example whose heights are printed, (6) = 0.4, 0.4, 0.5, 1, 1, 1 (Sec. 2.3), lies on the 0.1 sampling grid of the database, so it may be in the training data [inferred]. No author named Jun Wang (a J. Wang appears only in cited references). retest_candidate false: no public code. Screening code was I-SPEED.
